title: Health-Related Determinants of Internal Migration Among Older Adults in Canada: A Scoping Review
content: Existing sources of evidence cite a wide array of motivations for older adults’ migration/residential relocation within Canadian borders, including health-related issues. However, there is limited research on health as a motivation for older adults’ migration/residential relocation. This review explores the role of the internal mobility of older adults in Canada for health-related reasons, with a particular focus on the rural-urban axis. Sources of evidence addressing migration/relocation within Canadian borders – regardless of distance moved – were included. Changes of residence into long-term or assisted living, and seasonal migration, were excluded. Of the 3165 documents screened, 17 were chosen for analysis. The results consistently suggest that older adults with a history of poor health or high healthcare needs are more likely to relocate than their healthier counterparts. Relocation occurs more often towards small or mid-sized urban centres than to large metropolitan areas. While involuntary relocations are likely to produce adverse outcomes, preventing desired moves can also have negative consequences for the health and well-being of involuntary stayers.
